newsitem.title: USA: Most Woolworth ex-employees seen finding new jobs.
newsitem.headline: Most Woolworth ex-employees seen finding new jobs.

text.p: If there is a silver lining to be found in the closing of the more than 400 Woolworth Corp stores, it is that the U.S. economy and labor market are healthy, and most of the 9,200 employees who will be laid off should be able to find new jobs, economists said.

Since the beginning of the year, more than 150,000 retailing jobs have been created, according to U.S. government figues. But including Woolworth there have only been about 29,000 announced layoffs, according to Chicago-based outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
"To absorb these people should be easier than otherwise because the economy is operating with tight labor markets," said Neal Soss, chief economist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
Yet, the operative word is easier, not easy, despite a low 5.0-percent unemployment rate.
Even as service sector job growth soars, retail trade employment is its weakest component. As such, the retail share of service jobs has fallen to 28.4 percent from 28.7 percent at the end of 1995.
"In this economy, even with the low unemployment rate, you still have massive restructurings going on," said Robert Brusca, chief economist at The Nikko Securities Co International Inc.

Indeed, in announcing the closing of Woolworth stores after 117 years in business, the company also said it would convert 100 stores into Foot Locker or Champs Sports, which are owned by Woolworth. But a company spokesman said that while the laid off employees can interview for the positions, the skills are different, so it's not a given they would be rehired.
"The job market is tight enough that they will get new jobs," said Brusca. "But these are people who will start at the bottom rung. They leave their seniority and seniority premiums behind.
"The skilled workers have a better chance, since the labor market is marked by shortages in skilled jobs," he added.
Much also depends on regional economic factors, experts said.
Since the Midwest is booming, analysts figure those laid off in the 13 Chicago stores should find work more quickly.
But in New York, where 60 Woolworth stores will close, retail job growth is anemic, said John Tepper Marlin, chief economist in the city's comptroller's office.

Only 4,500 retail jobs have been created in New York City since January and 4,600 over the past year, he said, which may make it tough for Woolworth's 1,165 employees (500 of whom are full-time) to find new jobs.
In addition, more stores are closing than opening, Marlin said, although the stores that are opening are "mega-stores."
"But the new stores do not necessarily create more jobs," he said, "because new stores are much more efficient.
